He looked out the window. There was no doubt. The tree WAS closer to the house than it was yesterday. And why was it decorated with Christmas ornaments? Strange thing for a hot July afternoon. Another deep sip of the whiskey and the thought faded. He wondered what happened to the dog. Was there a dog? He seemed to remember one. Maybe he was just thinking about his partner's old coat. Another sip and the tree became blurry. Ah, the partner. What was their name? Did it matter? They were gone and mostly forgotten. He did remember the gleam in their eye as he fitted the last brick in the cellar wall sealing them in. He smiled. Didn't they make a movie out of it? Probably. Another sip and the glass was empty. He sighed and went to the kitchen. The large drum of whiskey sat next to the refrigerator like a sullen bank guard. He pumped out enough to fill the tumbler. He kicked the barrel and made a hollow THUMP sound. Almost empty. Good thing he had five full ones in the pantry. He turned back to the living room. He saw an empty dog dish by the door. There WAS a dog! What happened to him? He tried to remember but all that came to mind was his father glaring at him as he failed yet another attempt to harm the vagrant that his father had brought home for practice. He could still hear the sharp report of the revolver as his dad shot the man. He still resented those training sessions. Asking an eight-year-old boy to harm a grown man seemed highly unreasonable, but Father was an unreasonable man. He thought about him. Wondering where he was. He'd be about seventy now. Thirty years and no contact save for a monthly postcard with the lyrics to a cheerful song written in blood. Father was still proud of his political beliefs. And Mother. Most women would be aghast if they found their son wearing her new dress, but not Mother. She grabbed his arm and drove him into town and made him go into a department store and buy matching shoes. Ah, Mother. Still sitting behind the wheel of the old car lo these many years. He really should pour gasoline on it and set it on fire or maybe use some of that excess whiskey. 

He sat in the recliner and realized that the Christmas tree was now in the living room. And the dog was standing on its back legs next to it. The dog was wearing a three-piece suit. The tie was knotted immaculately and a handkerchief was folded neatly in the jacket pocket. The dog said something, but he didn't speak the language so the dog used semaphore flags. The message was clear. The tree was an ambassador from a place both very close yet quite far away. He was to finish his drink and accompany it. He closed his eyes and nodded. He hated Tuesdays.
